Apple’s new “intelligent personal hub” strategy is about much more than the iPhone. Also: The company makes job cuts at Fitness+ while it ponders the future of the service, here’s what happened to the iPhone Duo Pencil and the launch of Apple Pay in India is imminent.

Last week in _Power On_: Apple’s iPhone Duo will help make foldables [the new normal](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-09-13/apple-s-iphone-duo-will-make-foldable-phones-the-new-normal-apple-store-revamp-mtzvsb60).

### The Starters

Apple CEO John Ternus describes his “intelligent personal hub” approach.Source: Apple Inc.

When John Ternus kicked off his first keynote presentation as Apple Inc.’s new chief executive officer this month, he used the first few minutes to articulate his vision for the future of devices in the artificial intelligence era.

He asked viewers to imagine designing an ideal AI device from scratch. Such a product would require an always-on internet connection, a decent-sized display, top-tier cameras and microphones, and great battery life. It would need to be easy to use and work with other hardware, software and services, Ternus said.

He wanted the audience to feel as though he was about to introduce a breakthrough device — something that would compete with the growing range of AI-centric gadgets. His speech was so convincing that many at Apple thought he was about to introduce the company’s [upcoming new AI hub](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-28/new-apple-tv-4k-box-homepod-mini-and-siri-ai-smart-home-hub-are-coming) for the home.

But his point was actually quite different. In his view, the perfect AI device already exists: the iPhone itself. It’s no surprise Ternus would say this. With OpenAI [about to launch its AI-first computer](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-06/what-is-openai-s-device-a-doughnut-shaped-speaker-that-costs-over-300) and Apple lacking a revolutionary new mobile product, the latest iPhone models are the best showcase for Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. In other words, Ternus is playing his only hand.

When something does eventually replace the iPhone as the core offering in consumer electronics, he’ll probably adopt another worldview. But for now, expect Ternus to keep discussing this “intelligent personal hub” approach — with the smartphone becoming an ever-more important part of Apple’s ecosystem. Want the cool new Apple [smart glasses next fall](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-07-26/apple-glasses-may-debut-at-wwdc-2027-privacy-camera-features-versus-meta-ms1v7lta)? You’ll need an iPhone. Those [AirPods with cameras](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-19/apple-s-camera-equipped-ai-airpods-remain-on-track-for-2027-despite-video-leak)? You guessed it: an iPhone.

How long will this phone-centric world last? Longer than many people think. We may reach a point when augmented reality glasses can replace an iPhone, once they can pack enough processing and cloud computing power into a lightweight package. But that’s many years away. For now, the AI-powered iPhone is the center of everything.

But in making the case for an intelligent personal hub, Ternus left room for other devices to take a major role. That includes the smart home screen that Apple is finally set to be introduced as early as next month. It promises to be one of the most anticipated launches of Ternus’ early tenure, alongside the [iPhone Duo](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-09-13/apple-s-iphone-duo-will-make-foldable-phones-the-new-normal-apple-store-revamp-mtzvsb60) and a still-pending [touch-screen MacBook](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-26/apple-s-touchscreen-macbook-to-use-m5-pro-max-chips-m7-pro-max-models-in-2027).

While the iPhone anchors a person’s mobile life, the smart display will serve as a [hub for the home](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-11-12/apple-home-hub-detailed-apple-intelligence-homeos-square-ipad-like-design). The pitch: It will bring together all of your connected-device controls, video calls, intercom capabilities and media, while giving you access to Apple services and apps. It also will feature a new operating system built around Siri AI.

The Amazon Echo Show.Photographer: Chris Welch/Bloomberg

The device, dubbed J490 inside Apple, is being tested widely in employees’ homes on its way to a release. The product checks many of the boxes in Ternus’ description of an intelligent personal hub. It has pervasive connectivity through home Wi-Fi, an advanced display, a camera, microphones, and an easy-to-use interface that looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS. It also syncs with an iPhone for setup and various other tasks.

The roughly square screen will come in versions that either sit on a stand — resembling a HomePod mini chopped in half — or attach to a wall. It’s most similar to an Amazon.com Inc. Echo Show, but with a considerably smaller screen. One major feature will be facial recognition through the front-facing camera system, which allows the display to identify who is looking at it and personalize what appears, including apps, notes, calendar appointments, news, music and podcasts.

As an aside, Apple’s ability to pull this off without a standard Face ID-level depth sensor gives me confidence that the company could eventually bring facial recognition to the iPhone Duo (which currently relies on fingerprint-based Touch ID) even without the physical space typically required. Still, it will need to overcome the security challenges that might arise if it’s too easy to unlock a phone.

The display will have its own home screen, widgets and clock faces similar to those on an Apple Watch or in the iPhone Duo’s upgraded StandBy mode. But the killer feature is Siri. Apple had [planned a debut](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-11-12/apple-home-hub-detailed-apple-intelligence-homeos-square-ipad-like-design) as far back as 2024, but [couldn’t launch it until](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-09/apple-postpones-smart-home-display-launch-as-it-waits-for-new-ai-and-siri) the assistant’s AI capabilities were ready. That finally happened this month, when [Siri AI was formally released](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-06-14/siri-ai-hands-on-review-ios-27-macos-27-details-iphone-fold-touch-macbook) as part of iOS 27.

Apple imagines people using Siri on the home hub to look up information across their devices and accounts. They could ask it to play a podcast or song someone sent them a while ago, find a particular image to display, or carry out more precise tasks in apps like Notes, Reminders and Calendar. The Siri AI app will also let them conduct more complex searches within an Apple interface.

When Steve Jobs ran Apple, he made it clear that the company needed to own the three main settings in which people spend their time: at home, on the go and in the car. Under Ternus, the iPhone remains the anchor for mobile life, while the long-awaited home hub will give Apple a more central role in the household (alongside the new HomePod mini and TV set-top box with Siri AI).

The car remains the unresolved piece, with no apparent winning solution beyond the CarPlay interface. Apple famously spent a decade building a self-driving car before [killing it in early 2024](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-02-27/apple-cancels-work-on-electric-car-shifts-team-to-generative-ai). Less known is the fact that Ternus was one of the biggest voices inside Apple against the project. As he puts his stamp on the first two areas, we’ll see whether he can chart a path for this vital third segment.

### The Bench

Apple’s iPhone Duo.Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg

**Here’s what happened with the iPhone Duo Pencil.**I [reported a few weeks before](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-08-30/john-ternus-management-team-apple-watch-series-12-foldable-iphone-apple-pencil-mtfvmdyu) Apple’s big [iPhone Duo launch](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-09-13/apple-s-iphone-duo-will-make-foldable-phones-the-new-normal-apple-store-revamp-mtzvsb60) event that the company had tested a new Pencil stylus for the product — something that was shorter and magnetic, so it could attach to the device’s hinge. This was a controversial move. After all, Steve Jobs famously said that no one wanted to use a stylus with a phone.

At the time, I said the accessory was unlikely to actually be unveiled, and that was correct. Instead, Apple designed the Duo to support the iPad’s Pencil on its external and interior screens. Here’s what happened: The original plan was to introduce the Pencil designed for the Duo but, a few months ago, the accessory ran into technical problems ahead of mass production. Apple then pivoted to just supporting the iPad versions of the accessory.

But getting the iPad Pencils to work on the iPhone Duo isn’t as simple as hitting a button to enable support. Apple has to roll out new software to make them compatible and run loads of internal tests. That process is now underway within Apple, with the company — as it said during the Duo unveiling — believing that support will be ready by the end of the year. I would take that literally: It will be fairly late in 2026.

Apple Fitness+.Source: Apple Inc.

**Apple makes job cuts at Fitness+, indicating changing priorities for the service.**I [reported](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-02-08/apple-readies-iphone-17e-new-siri-entry-level-ipad-ipad-air-and-macbook-pro-mldr3hpk) earlier this year that Apple was reevaluating its Fitness+ platform, a competitor to Peloton content that’s now overseen by services chief Eddy Cue and health leader Sumbul Desai. I don’t believe, as of this second, that the service is on the chopping block, but given the considerable costs, ever-present demand for new content and subscriber churn rates, it’s an easy place for Apple to look to make cuts. And that is starting now.

This past week, I’m told, Apple enacted another round of [increasingly common](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-21/apple-cuts-jobs-in-siri-vision-pro-immersive-video-and-gaming-teams) layoffs by cutting a handful of employees working on Fitness+. The affected workers included staff who contributed to the audio side of the service — things like the [Time to Walk and Time to Run](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102128 "Use Time to Walk or Time to Run - Apple Support") audio sessions you can listen to from your Apple Watch without watching a video. Though new releases for audio content will drop in frequency, they’re not going away completely — as of now.

Still, this is widely seen within the Fitness+ organization as the beginning of more drastic cost-cutting measures and other major changes to the service in the months and years ahead. My bet is that Apple eventually integrates Fitness+ into the revamped Health app — now that both these functions are part of the same operation. Already, Apple is adding video clips to the upcoming Health app revamp to explain certain topics and benchmarks.

### Overtime

Snap Specs.Photographer: Chris Welch/Bloomberg

### Post Game Q&A

Q: _What’s new in the latest iOS betas?_  
A: Apple delivered the first 27.2 beta versions of its major operating systems this past week, and they came with some notable changes. First, while Apple says its new Health app will come in a later release, it is using iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 to test it early with developers and others in the company’s beta programs. There’s also support for user profiles in the Apple TV app for the first time, outside of tvOS, as well as support for more languages for Siri AI. As for why Apple is distributing 27.2 rather than 27.1, it appears that the .1 release is exclusive to the iPhone Duo. For anyone looking to get a Duo, I’d be wary at this point of testing iOS 27.2 — the differing version numbers could make things more complicated when you’re setting up that device [come Oct. 23](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-09-10/iphone-duo-hands-on-apple-s-first-foldable-phone-makes-strong-first-impression).

Q: _Do you think next year’s second-generation iPhone Duo will be a redesign?_  
A: That seems unlikely. I think it’s time to get used to Apple rolling out a product design and sticking to it for a long time. Take the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro, which have gone half a decade with their current designs. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 has the same design as the first model from 2022, and the AirPods have looked essentially identical for years. There aren’t a lot of quick upgrades coming out of Apple’s design department at the moment. That’s a big change from the old days. In four successive years, Apple launched four entirely new tablet designs: the 2010 original iPad, the 2011 iPad 2, the 2012 iPad mini and the 2013 iPad Air. But in the current environment, I don’t expect Apple to suddenly put the pedal to the metal and redesign the iPhone Duo in only 12 months.
